entries: Circa 1600, from Middle Low German kabbelouw (14th c.), from Middle Dutch cabbeliau, cabelliau (12th c.), from Old Dutch cabillau, possibly from Latin baculum (“stick, staff”), referring to the way cod were split and dried on wooden sticks. Or, with metathesis from/influenced by Basque bakailao (“cod”), Portuguese bacalhau (“cod”). The contemporary form was probably reinforced by modern Dutch kabeljauw against variants like Kabbelau, Kabliau.

entries:
From Middle High German liederlich (“frivolous”, originally "slack, weak"), which Kluge compares to Ancient Greek ἐλεύθερος (eleútheros, “free”) (from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ- (“to grow”)). Pokorny prefers a derivation from Proto-Indo-European *(s)lew- (“slack; loose; limp”), see also Old Norse slokna (“to go out”).
Compare Old Norse loddari (“juggler; tramp”), Old High German lotar (“vain; void; insignificant”), Dutch lodder (“a wanton”), Old English loddere (“pauper, beggar”) and English lither. See also lotterig (“slovenly”) and lottern (“lead a slovenly life”). Not related to Luder.

entries: Frequentative of Middle High German verzetten (“to scatter, disperse”), from ver- + Old High German zetten (“to spread”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *tadjaną (“to strew, scatter”).
